summary: Jesus sets His face toward Jerusalem. Refused by a Samaritan village, He rebukes James and John’s call for fire and tells would-be followers the cost.
key_insight: Luke marks the turning point of his Gospel by its goal: “the time had come for Him to be received up.” The cross was still months away, but Jesus “steadfastly set His face” toward it, and from here to chapter 19 Luke tells his story as one long road to Jerusalem.
story: The time had come for Jesus to be received up, and He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem. He sent messengers ahead of Him, and they went into a village of the Samaritans to prepare for Him.
But the people there did not receive Him, “because His face was set for the journey to Jerusalem.”

When His disciples James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, do You want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, just as Elijah did?” But Jesus turned and rebuked them: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy men’s lives but to save them.” And they went on to another village.

As they journeyed on the road, a man said to Him, “Lord, I will follow You wherever You go.” Jesus answered, “Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.”
To another He said, “Follow Me.” The man answered, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” Jesus said to him, “Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and preach the kingdom of God.”

Another said, “Lord, I will follow You, but let me first go and bid them farewell who are at my house.” Jesus said to him, “No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”

fit.question: This timeline joins Luke’s departure to Jesus’ journey to the Feast of Tabernacles, which John says He made “not openly, but as it were in secret” (John 7:10; event 92). Yet Luke has messengers going ahead to prepare for Him. Can these be the same journey?

points.label: Not the public show
points.text: Jesus’ brothers had urged Him to go to Judea and show Himself to the world (John 7:3–4). He refused, and went up only after they had gone. McGarvey and Edersheim read “in secret” as the opposite of that public display: Jesus did not travel with the crowds of festival pilgrims. Sending messengers ahead to find lodging for Himself and the Twelve fits a quiet journey of that kind.

points.label: Another placement
points.text: Some harmonies place Luke 9:51 later instead, with Jesus’ final departure from Galilee (Matthew 19:1; Mark 10:1), and read Luke’s journey as more than one trip gathered under one heading. Luke names no feast and gives no date, so the question cannot be settled from his text alone.

fit.note: Luke and John each describe a real journey; the only open question is whether they describe the same one, and neither account needs correcting to answer it.
fit.short: Jesus may have gone up apart from the pilgrim crowds, with messengers seeking lodging. Some harmonies place Luke’s departure later instead.

fit.question: Luke sets two of these conversations on the road toward Jerusalem. Matthew sets them much earlier, by the Sea of Galilee before the storm (Matthew 8:19–22; event 66). When did they happen?

points.label: More than one volunteer
points.text: Many people offered to follow Jesus. In Matthew the first man is a scribe who calls Him “Teacher,” and Jesus says “Follow Me” after the second man’s request; in Luke the volunteer says “Lord,” and Jesus says “Follow Me” first. Jesus may well have given the same hard answers on more than one day, and Luke records a third man Matthew does not mention.

points.label: Joined by subject
points.text: McGarvey suggests the first conversation happened where Matthew places it and the others where Luke places them, each writer setting a like incident beside his own because they teach the same lesson. Luke links his scenes loosely (“as they journeyed on the road,” 9:57) and gives no dates.

fit.note: Neither writer claims these words were spoken only once, and repeating a hard saying is just what a traveling teacher would do.
fit.short: Jesus may have given these hard answers more than once, or a writer set a similar conversation beside his own because it taught the same lesson.

scene.label: The road through Samaria
scene.text: Luke names no feast, but this timeline, with McGarvey and Edersheim, sets the journey in early autumn, on the way to the Feast of Tabernacles. The direct road from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria, about three days’ walk according to Josephus, who says Galileans commonly took it to the feasts. He also tells of Galilean pilgrims attacked in Samaria on their way to a feast.

scene.label: Samaritans and Jerusalem
scene.text: Samaritans held that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, was the place to worship (John 4:20). A teacher whose face was set for the Jerusalem feast was not welcome to stay the night.

scene.label: Elijah’s fire
scene.text: James and John were thinking of 2 Kings 1:9–12, where Elijah called down fire on soldiers sent by the king who ruled from Samaria. Jesus had named these brothers “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17).

scene.label: Burial and the plow
scene.text: Burying a father was a sacred duty. The man may have meant his father had just died, or that he wanted to stay home until his father’s death; Luke does not say. The plow saying recalls Elisha, called from his plowing, who asked to kiss his parents goodbye before following Elijah (1 Kings 19:19–21).

scene.label: Words not in every manuscript
scene.text: Many of the oldest manuscripts do not have “just as Elijah did” (v. 54) or Jesus’ saying that begins “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of” (vv. 55–56). The NKJV includes them; many other translations place them in a footnote.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this departure, and he makes it the hinge of his Gospel: from here to 19:27 he follows Jesus on the road to Jerusalem, gathering teaching and parables found nowhere else. “Received up” looks beyond the cross to the Ascension, and the set face recalls the Servant who says, “I have set My face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7). Luke, who also wrote Acts, later tells how John went to Samaria to pray for Samaritan believers to receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17).

seeing.reveals: Jesus walks toward Jerusalem knowing what waits there, and neither rejection nor His disciples’ anger turns Him aside. He came to save lives, not to destroy them.
seeing.living: Jesus does not lower the cost to gain a follower. Following Him means putting His kingdom ahead of comfort and even family duty, without looking back. And those who follow a Savior whose face is set toward the cross cannot call down fire on the people who refuse Him.
seeing.ponder: What are you saying “first” about, before you will follow Jesus all the way?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus set His face toward the cross; He calls followers who will not look back.
preaching.watch_for: The word “face” frames the opening (vv. 51, 52, 53): Jesus sets His face, sends messengers before His face, and is refused because His face is set for Jerusalem. The section ends with a man looking back (v. 62); Jesus never does.
